newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ST Aerospace to return surplus cash.
newsitem.headline: ST Aerospace to return surplus cash.

text.p: Singapore Technologies Aerospace Ltd currently has surplus cash of about Singapore $30 million which it would distribute to shareholders by year-end, said group president and chief executive Boon Swan Foo.

Speaking to reporters on Monday at a briefing on interim results, Boon said: "Where we have surplus capital which cannot be effectively employed, we would like to return it to shareholders. We are in the process of reviewing our capital structure."

The group also declared for the first time an interim dividend of five percent because of its strong half year results where net profit more than tripled to S$28.01 million from last year's S$6.86 million.
Boon said he expected the group's strong performance to be sustained in the second half, which would bring full-year profit to around S$56 million.
The group's results were sharply above analysts' expectations of about S$36 million for the full year.
Elaborating on the group's surplus cash, group financial controller Patrick Lee said ST Aerospace's cash was around Singapore $400 million at the end of last year.
But after taking into account its various investment commitments and plans, surplus cash currently stood at S$30 million.
Boon said the surplus would be returned to shareholders, probably in the form of dividends, by year-end if no other investment opportunities arose.
He said the move to return surplus cash was part of the group's policy of using economic value added (EVA) measures to determine profit after deducting the cost of capital.

EVA for the first half of 1997 after accounting for the group's weighted average cost of capital of 10.3 percent was S$2.9 million, a significant improvement over a 1996 first half negative EVA of S$15.3 million.
On the group's prospects, Boon said the group expected to maintain annual profit growth of 15-20 percent profit from 1998.
He said the current upswing in aircraft maintenance hourly rates was expected to continue for the next five to seven years.
The group will be expanding its capacity by 20-30 percent in the U.S. through ST Mobile Aerospace Engineering with an additional wide-body hanger before the end of the year.
In Singapore, the group is also looking at expanding capacity but it is currently hampered by a lack of skilled man-power, Boon said.
